summary: Stateful PCE extensions let a PCE control MPLS traffic engineering paths that clients already have. This document extends PCEP so a PCE can itself start the setup of a new label switched path, instead of only reacting to a client's request.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8281 lets a path-computation server ask a router to create or remove a traffic-engineering path. The router reports the result and gives the server control of a path it creates.

subtitle: Extensions that let a path-computation server start and remove traffic-engineering paths on a router.

tldr.problem: Stateful PCE extensions let a Path Computation Element control locally configured paths, but dynamic networks also need it to create and remove paths on demand.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8281 adds a PCInitiate message and capability flags so a PCE can ask a Path Computation Client to create or delete an LSP, then receive reports about its state.
tldr.outcome: The extension enables PCE-initiated LSP setup using RSVP-TE and defines controls for delegation, cleanup, and resource limits. RFC 8281 is updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 8281 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9756. It defines PCE-initiated LSP procedures using RSVP-TE.

sections.title: From Advice to PCE-Initiated Paths
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a Path Computation Element (PCE) communicate about Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths (TE LSPs). Earlier stateful extensions focused on paths configured on the PCC and delegated to a PCE.

RFC 8281 adds setup, maintenance, and teardown of PCE-initiated LSPs without local configuration on the PCC. The RFC describes uses such as creating a path for an application request, adjusting aggregate bandwidth with several paths, and engineering traffic distribution. The decision when to create or delete a path is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A PCE can do more than calculate a path that a router already knows about. With this extension, it can ask a router to create a path and later ask it to remove that path.

sections.title: Agreeing to PCE-Initiated Setup
sections.content:
During PCEP session setup, both speakers use the STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV in an Open message to advertise support. RFC 8281 adds the I flag, called LSP-INSTANTIATION-CAPABILITY. A PCE can initiate LSPs only for a PCC that advertised this capability, and the PCC follows these procedures only when the PCE advertised it too.

This exchange lets each side know that the other supports the new path-instantiation procedures before either side uses them.
sections.plainLanguage: The PCE and router must both advertise support during session setup. A PCE can start paths only for a router that has agreed to this capability.

sections.title: The PCInitiate Request
sections.content:
The new PCInitiate message has Message-Type 12 and MUST include an SRP object and an LSP object. It may contain other objects. A message can carry a list of requests, each of which asks for an instantiation or deletion.

The SRP object contains an identifier unique within the PCEP session. The PCE increments it before each PCInitiate message, and the PCC echoes it in resulting error and report messages so the PCE can match responses to requests. The new R flag is clear for creation and set for removal.
sections.plainLanguage: Each PCInitiate message carries a request number and an LSP description. The PCE uses the number to identify the router's reply, while a flag says whether the request creates or removes the path.

sections.title: Creating, Updating, and Deleting an LSP
sections.content:
For creation, the request uses reserved PLSP-ID 0, includes a SYMBOLIC-PATH-NAME TLV, and MUST contain an Explicit Route Object (ERO). It may include endpoint information and attributes. This document specifies RSVP-TE for setting up the LSP; other setup methods are outside its scope.

After successful setup, the PCC assigns a non-zero PLSP-ID and sends a PCRpt with the Create and Delegate flags set. Later updates use PCUpd messages and that PLSP-ID. If required information is missing, a name is already in use, or parameters are unacceptable, the PCC reports an error.

For deletion, the PCE sends PCInitiate with the target PLSP-ID and the R flag set. A PLSP-ID of zero requests removal of all PCE-initiated LSPs delegated to that PCE. After removal, the PCC reports the removed state and echoes the request identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: To create a path, the PCE supplies a name and route, and the router assigns the path its identifier. To remove it, the PCE sends a request naming that identifier and the router reports the deletion.

sections.title: Delegation, Recovery, and Synchronization
sections.content:
The PCC MUST delegate a newly created PCE-initiated LSP to the PCE and MUST NOT revoke that delegation during an active session. If the PCE returns control or its session fails and the redelegation timer expires, the LSP can become an orphan while the state-timeout timer runs.

The original PCE or a backup can take control of an orphaned LSP by sending a PCInitiate message with its PLSP-ID. If the state-timeout timer expires, local policy determines whether the PCC removes the path or restores operator-defined default parameters; the PCC must support removal.

During state synchronization, the PCC reports its LSPs to the PCE and marks PCE-initiated ones with the Create flag. After synchronization, the PCE should request missing paths or remove unwanted ones, though the RFC notes that a deployment may delay or avoid this to protect active flows.
sections.plainLanguage: If a PCE session fails, paths are not removed immediately. A PCE can take control again during the recovery period; otherwise the router applies its local cleanup policy when the timer expires.

sections.title: Resource and Request Limits
sections.content:
A malicious or compromised PCE could send many instantiation requests and consume resources on a PCC or throughout the network. Rapid changes to paths can also cause repeated flaps. A PCC can limit the number of PCE-initiated LSPs or the resources allocated to them, and can limit how often operations occur.

A malicious or overloaded PCC could ignore requests and use PCE resources because the PCE keeps state for initiated LSPs. The PCE can limit pending requests or wait time, and may close the session or remove paths it initiated.
sections.plainLanguage: A PCE could overwhelm a router by asking for too many paths, while an unresponsive router could make the PCE keep waiting. The RFC describes limits and timeouts to control both problems.
